intro: Every recipe is really an instruction about heat: how much, from where, for how long, with or without water. A pan that is not hot enough turns a sauté into a stew. A crowded sheet pan turns a roast into a steam bath. A cheap cut of beef grilled like a steak is a jaw workout, and the same cut left for three hours under a lid falls apart into the best dinner of the week. Once you can see heat moving, most of the mystery of why a dish went wrong disappears, and so does most of the fear of cooking without a recipe.

This unit starts with the three ways heat travels in a kitchen: by touch, through moving air and water, and across open space from a glowing element. From there you will learn the dry-heat methods that brown, the moist-heat methods that soften, and the combination methods that do both, along with the two chemical changes behind browning and the reason a wet or crowded pan never gets there. Then you will learn to match method to food: which cuts want ten minutes of high heat and which want an afternoon of low, how to read a label at the meat counter, what each oven temperature does, and how to braise, stir-fry and build a pan sauce step by step.

Through all of it runs one tool and one set of numbers. The food thermometer, pushed into the thickest part of the food, is the only honest judge of doneness, and the USDA safe minimum temperatures, 165 °F for poultry, 160 °F for ground meat, 145 °F with a rest for whole cuts and fish, are the standard. By the end you will be able to look at any ingredient, choose a method, set a temperature, plan the time, and know when it is done.
bigQuestion: How does understanding the way heat moves let a cook choose the right method for any food and get it right the first time?

timeline.t: People cook over open fires, roasting food on sticks and hot stones: dry, radiant heat
Clay pots make boiling and stewing possible, adding moist heat to the cook's tools
Egyptians bake bread in clay ovens, cooking with hot air on every side
Abraham Darby patents a way to cast iron cooking pots in sand molds, making lidded pots cheap
Count Rumford studies heat and designs enclosed kitchen ranges that use far less fuel
James Sharp patents a gas stove in England, giving cooks a flame they can adjust instantly
An all-electric model kitchen is shown at the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago
Fannie Farmer's Boston Cooking-School Cook Book gives oven temperatures and exact measurements
French chemist Louis-Camille Maillard describes the browning reaction between sugars and amino acids
The first commercial microwave oven, the Radarange, goes on sale to restaurants
A countertop microwave oven for home kitchens is introduced
Convection ovens and instant-read thermometers are common, and the USDA publishes safe minimum temperatures

words.d: heat moving directly from one thing into another that it touches, such as pan to steak
heat carried by a moving liquid or gas, such as boiling water or oven air
heat traveling in straight lines from a hot source to whatever faces it, like a broiler
cooking with hot air, hot metal or hot fat and no added liquid: roasting, grilling, sautéing
cooking in or over liquid: boiling, simmering, poaching, steaming
brown food, then cook it slowly, covered, in a small amount of liquid until tender
the browning reaction between proteins and sugars on hot, dry food that creates roasted flavor
the browning of sugar itself at high heat, giving amber color and nutty flavor
overfilling a pan so steam cannot escape and the food steams instead of browning
the tough web in working muscles that turns to gelatin only with long, gentle, moist cooking
to add liquid to a hot pan and scrape up the browned fond for a sauce or braise
the rise in a meat's internal temperature after it leaves the heat, finished during resting

test.q: Which heat-transfer method surrounds pasta with water at 212 °F on every side?
test.why: Boiling water is a moving liquid carrying heat: convection.

test.q: A steak browns only on the side touching the pan. That is an example of which kind of heat transfer?
test.why: Conduction moves heat by direct contact. Only the surface touching the hot metal receives it.

test.q: Why does a broiler cook only the top of the food?
choices: Radiant heat travels in straight lines to the side facing the element
The air in the oven is cold
test.why: A broiler is radiant heat from above, so only the surface facing it browns.

test.q: Vegetables piled deep on one sheet pan come out pale and limp. What happened?
choices: They steamed in their own moisture because the pan was crowded
test.why: Trapped steam holds the surface at about 212 °F, where nothing browns.

test.q: Which of the following is a moist-heat method?
test.why: Poaching cooks food gently in liquid below boiling. The others use dry heat.

test.q: What makes braising a combination method?
choices: It browns with dry heat and then finishes with moist heat under a lid
It uses both an oven and a microwave
test.why: A braise sears first, then simmers covered in liquid, using both kinds of heat in order.

test.q: Which molecules react in the Maillard reaction?
test.why: Maillard browning is the reaction between proteins (amino acids) and sugars on a hot, dry surface.

test.q: Why can food never brown while it sits in water?
choices: The surface cannot get hotter than 212 °F while water is present
Water makes the pan too heavy
test.why: Browning needs dry heat well above the boiling point, and water caps the surface at 212 °F.

test.q: Which cut is the right choice for a three-hour braise?
test.why: Chuck is a working muscle full of connective tissue, which slow moist heat turns to gelatin.

test.q: What must ground beef reach to be safe?
test.why: USDA: ground beef, pork and lamb to 160 °F. Grinding spreads surface bacteria throughout.

test.q: A pork chop reads 145 °F. What is the USDA rule?
test.why: Whole cuts of pork, beef, lamb and veal are safe at 145 °F followed by a 3-minute rest.

test.q: In a stir-fry, why does the chicken cook first and alone?
choices: Vegetables must be cooked last for color only
Cooking in batches keeps the pan hot enough to brown
Chicken must be added to a cold pan
test.why: Everything at once crowds the pan and drops the heat. Batches keep it searing.

test.q: Where should a food thermometer go in a roast?
choices: Into the thickest part, away from bone and pan
test.why: Bone and metal read high. The center of the thickest meat is the last place to reach temperature.

test.q: What does resting meat after cooking accomplish?
choices: The juices settle and the temperature finishes rising
The meat cools to a safe temperature
The bacteria are killed by the foil
test.why: Resting lets carryover cooking finish and the juices redistribute so they stay in the slices.

test.q: Which step is required before simmering dried red kidney beans?
choices: Cooking on low in a slow cooker
A full rolling boil for at least 10 minutes
test.why: Raw kidney beans contain a toxin that only a hard 10-minute boil destroys; a slow cooker does not get hot enough.

write.prompt: Plan a dinner built around a tough cut of meat and a vegetable side. Write the steps in order, from the meat counter to the table, and for each step name the cooking method, the heat setting or oven temperature, the tool, and the safe temperature or time rule it depends on. Then explain why each step is there.
tips: Put the steps in order, including preheating and resting.
Name the tool for each step: Dutch oven, sheet pan, thermometer, tongs.
Say which kind of heat each step uses and why that food needs it.
Include the USDA temperature for the meat and the two-hour rule for leftovers.
Check the numbers: ratios, times and temperatures must add up.
